01_vector_dot.title: Dot Products as Similarity
01_vector_dot.description:
Many ML computations reduce to weighted sums, and the dot product is the basic example.

```python
a = [1, 2]
b = [3, 4]
```

The dot product multiplies aligned components and sums the results.

q2.question: Why does the dot product appear so often in ML models?
options: It measures weighted alignment between vectors and forms the core of linear layers.
It is only used for image resizing.
It automatically normalizes all features to unit length.
explanations: Yes. Linear models and neural layers rely on weighted sums constantly.
It is far more general than image resizing.
Normalization is a separate operation.
q2.answerReason: Scoring similarity and forming weighted combinations are central operations throughout ML.

02_perceptron.title: A Perceptron Applies Weights and a Threshold
02_perceptron.description:
A perceptron computes a weighted sum and then applies a decision rule.

```python
score = w1 * x1 + w2 * x2 + bias
```

q2.question: What changes when you adjust the bias?
options: It shifts the decision threshold without changing the input features themselves.
It sorts the training dataset before learning.
It removes the need for weights.
explanations: Correct. Bias shifts the activation boundary.
Sorting data is unrelated to bias.
Weights remain essential.
q2.answerReason: Bias lets a neuron activate even when all inputs are zero or stay off despite positive inputs.

03_gradient_descent.title: Gradient Descent Moves Opposite the Gradient
03_gradient_descent.description:
If the gradient points uphill, subtracting it moves parameters toward lower loss.

```python
weight = weight - lr * grad
```

q1.question: What is printed after one update?

q2.question: Why do we subtract the gradient during minimization?
options: Because the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase of the loss.
Because subtraction makes training deterministic on any dataset.
Because gradients are always negative numbers.
explanations: Yes. Moving opposite the gradient is the local downhill direction.
Determinism depends on many other factors.
Gradients can be positive, negative, or zero.
q2.answerReason: The sign matters: to reduce loss, update in the opposite direction from increasing loss.

04_softmax.title: Softmax Turns Logits into a Distribution
04_softmax.description:
Softmax converts arbitrary scores into positive values that sum to 1.

```python
probs = exp(logits) / sum(exp(logits))
```

That makes it useful for multiclass prediction.

q2.question: Why do larger logits get larger softmax probabilities?
options: Exponentiation preserves ordering and amplifies differences before normalization.
Softmax first sorts classes alphabetically.
Softmax clips all logits to the same value.
explanations: Correct. Bigger logits produce larger exponentials.
Class names do not determine probabilities.
Softmax does not flatten everything equally.
q2.answerReason: Normalization rescales the scores, but the exponential step is what makes higher logits dominate more strongly.

05_attention_scores.title: Attention Scores from Query and Key
05_attention_scores.description:
Attention starts by comparing a query vector with key vectors.

```python
score = q @ k
```

The larger the compatibility score, the more weight that token can receive after softmax.

q2.question: What does a larger query-key score usually mean?
options: The query is more aligned with that key, so that token can receive more attention weight.
The sequence becomes shorter.
The model skips the value vectors entirely.
explanations: Yes. The score ranks relevance before normalization.
Attention scores do not change sequence length directly.
Values are still needed to produce the mixed output.
q2.answerReason: Scores are not the final output; they decide how strongly each value vector contributes.

06_transformer_block.title: Residual Paths Preserve Signal
06_transformer_block.description:
Transformer blocks add residual connections so the layer can refine a representation instead of replacing it entirely.

```python
x = x + attention(x)
```

q2.question: Why are residual connections important in deep models?
options: They make it easier to preserve and refine information across many layers.
They remove the need for normalization and nonlinearities.
They force every layer to learn the exact same function.
explanations: Correct. Residuals help optimization and information flow.
Residuals complement, not replace, other components.
Layers can still learn different transformations.
q2.answerReason: Deep networks train more reliably when each layer can learn a correction on top of an existing signal.

07_training_loop.title: The Training Loop Repeats Forward, Loss, Backward, Step
07_training_loop.description:
Most model training repeats the same cycle: compute predictions, compute loss, backpropagate gradients, and update parameters.

```python
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
```

q2.question: Why does `optimizer.step()` come after `loss.backward()`?
options: The optimizer needs gradients computed from the backward pass before it can update weights.
Backward only works after the weights have already changed.
The order is arbitrary.
explanations: Yes. No gradients means no informed parameter update.
Backward computes gradients from the current forward pass first.
The order is not arbitrary.
q2.answerReason: Updates depend on gradients, so the graph must be differentiated before the optimizer changes parameters.

08_llm_next_token.title: LLMs Predict the Next Token Distribution
08_llm_next_token.description:
An LLM does not retrieve one hard-coded answer. It repeatedly predicts a probability distribution over the next token.

```text
context -> logits -> probabilities -> sampled/selected next token
```

q2.question: What is the model output immediately before token selection?
options: A vector of logits over the vocabulary.
A full paragraph string already chosen by the model.
The final training loss from the dataset.
explanations: Correct. Token selection happens from logits or their normalized probabilities.
The paragraph is built token by token, not emitted all at once.
Training loss is not the direct generation output.
q2.answerReason: Generation is incremental: each step produces scores for the next token, then the process repeats.
